steps.instructions: Power the bed on after it has been removed from patient use and confirm that the display shows Error 090 Call Service. Document when the error appears and whether brake-related indicators behave abnormally as the brake pedal is applied and released.

steps.title: Confirm Actual Brake Function Physically
steps.instructions: With the bed unloaded and positioned safely, apply the brakes and gently attempt to move the bed to confirm that the casters hold. Release the brakes and confirm that the bed rolls normally when intended. Inspect the visible pedal and linkage area for obvious damage or obstruction.

steps.title: Check Power Condition and Fault-Clearing Requirements
steps.instructions: Confirm appropriate power connection and note whether Error 090 remains displayed. Correct any identified brake-switch wiring or connection issue before cycling power, since the error may remain latched until the fault is corrected and power is cycled.

steps.title: Inspect Accessible Brake-Switch Wiring and Connections
steps.instructions: Remove power as appropriate and inspect accessible brake-switch wiring, harness routing, and connectors for looseness, disconnection, pinching, abrasion, damage, contamination, fluid intrusion, or damaged pins. Reseat accessible loose connectors when within normal Clinical Engineering repair scope.

steps.title: Isolate Whether the Fault Is Correctable Externally
steps.instructions: Correct visible accessible wiring, contamination, or connector issues when within repair scope. If no accessible cause is identified and Error 090 remains present, remove the bed from service for further repair or bench evaluation.

steps.title: Cycle Power and Verify Repair
steps.instructions: After correcting an identified accessible issue, power-cycle the bed and confirm that Error 090 Call Service no longer appears. Verify normal brake apply and release operation, stationary holding while braked, normal brake-status indication, and absence of related alerts before return to service.

CCR.Complaint: Stryker S3 hospital bed displayed Error 090 Call Service - Brake Switch Error during power-on evaluation. Brake-status indication was considered unreliable pending inspection.
CCR.Cause: Inspection identified a loose accessible brake-switch harness connection causing interruption of the brake-switch circuit. Error remained displayed until corrective action and power cycling were completed.
CCR.Resolution: Removed bed from patient use, verified physical brake holding function, reseated and secured the accessible brake-switch harness connection, cycled bed power, and confirmed Error 090 cleared. Verified normal brake apply/release operation and brake-status indication before returning the bed to service.

title: Stryker S3 Hospital Bed - Error: 103 Input Timer
description: Troubleshooting Error 103 Input Timer when a continuously active pendant, siderail, or footboard control input may affect reliable bed motion operation or contribute to unintended movement.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Remove the Stryker S3 bed from patient use if unintended movement occurs, bed motion is unavailable, or controls appear stuck or unreliable. If occupied, coordinate a safe transfer to another appropriate bed before troubleshooting motion controls.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm that the bed displays Error 103 Call Service and document the logged condition as InputTimer. With the bed unoccupied, observe whether the error returns and whether a motion command appears continuously active.

steps.title: Inspect the Pendant Control
steps.instructions: Inspect the pendant, if installed, for stuck keys, damaged overlays, contamination, fluid intrusion, cracked housing, damaged cabling, or connector issues. Confirm that each motion button releases normally.

steps.title: Inspect the Siderail Controls
steps.instructions: Inspect siderail motion-control panels for jammed buttons, damaged overlays, contamination, fluid intrusion, cracks, or abnormal button feel. Test each motion command individually and confirm motion stops when released.

steps.title: Inspect the Footboard Controls
steps.instructions: Check the footboard motion-control area for stuck keys, damage, contamination, or signs of impact. Test applicable commands individually and confirm no command remains active after release.

steps.title: Check External Connections and Cable Condition
steps.instructions: Inspect accessible pendant, siderail, and footboard control cabling and connectors for looseness, pin damage, strain, pinch damage, contamination, corrosion, or broken locking features. Reseat accessible external connectors when appropriate and safe.

steps.title: Isolate the Continuously Active Input
steps.instructions: When a specific external control location is suspected, isolate that external control assembly as appropriate for Clinical Engineering evaluation and retest the unoccupied bed. Do not return the bed to service with required controls disconnected or unavailable.

steps.title: Verify Operation After Correction
steps.instructions: After correcting an external cause, perform functional testing of all installed motion controls. Confirm each command stops immediately when released, no unintended motion occurs, and Error 103 does not return.

steps.title: Stop When Resolved
steps.instructions: When an external control, cable, connector, contamination issue, or jammed button has been corrected and the bed passes functional testing without recurrence, document the repair and return the bed to service according to facility procedure.

CCR.Complaint: Stryker S3 hospital bed displayed Error 103 Call Service - InputTimer. Staff reported abnormal bed motion control behavior with a suspected continuously active input.
CCR.Cause: Inspection identified a stuck pendant motion button with a damaged overlay, causing the bed to sense the input as continuously On and log Error 103.
CCR.Resolution: Removed bed from patient use, replaced the defective pendant, verified footboard, siderail, and pendant motion controls returned to neutral normally, and confirmed Error 103 did not recur during functional testing. Bed returned to service.

title: Stryker S3 Hospital Bed - Error: 102 Stuck Safety Relay
description: Troubleshooting Error 102 Stuck Safety Relay, which may cause unreliable or disabled bed motion when the safety relay remains active without a pressed control.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Remove the Stryker S3 bed from patient use if motion control cannot be trusted, motion is disabled, or unintended movement is possible. If occupied, coordinate a safe transfer to a known-working bed before troubleshooting.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Bed Behavior
steps.instructions: With the bed removed from clinical use, power the bed normally and confirm Error 102 Call Service. Document whether the error appears after approximately one minute without a motion button press, after startup, after use of a specific control location, or with abnormal bed motion. Do not rely only on Auto-Cycle Mode testing.

steps.title: Check the Power Source and Basic Bed Condition
steps.instructions: Verify connection to an appropriate grounded AC outlet. Inspect the power cord, plug, strain relief, exterior surfaces, and control areas for visible damage, liquid contamination, or cleaning-fluid intrusion. Use a known-good outlet if permitted by facility procedure.

steps.title: Inspect for a Physically Stuck Motion Button
steps.instructions: Inspect footboard, siderail, and pendant motion controls if installed. Press and release each motion-related button individually, looking for controls that remain depressed, feel sticky, fail to spring back, or appear damaged.

steps.title: Inspect Control Overlays and External Control Surfaces
steps.instructions: Examine footboard and siderail switch overlays for cracked, punctured, lifted, worn, contaminated, or distorted membrane surfaces. Do not perform internal disassembly during the initial troubleshooting evaluation.

steps.title: Inspect Pendant Controls and Accessible Cabling
steps.instructions: Inspect any connected pendant for stuck buttons, contamination, damage, or a pinched cable. Inspect accessible external cables and connectors for looseness, damage, bent pins, fluid contamination, or intermittent connection. Substitute or remove an accessory only when permitted by facility service practice.

steps.title: Retest the Bed Under Normal Motion-Control Conditions
steps.instructions: After addressing any external condition, restart the bed and leave all motion controls untouched for longer than one minute. Confirm whether Error 102 returns. If it does not return, test each available motion function and verify movement occurs only when intentionally commanded and stops when the control is released.

steps.title: Identify Need for Repair Evaluation
steps.instructions: If Error 102 returns after external controls, accessories, cables, connectors, contamination, power conditions, and obvious damage have been ruled out, remove the bed from service and send it for qualified bench evaluation according to approved service documentation.

steps.title: Verify Operation After Repair
steps.instructions: After correction or replacement of the failed accessory or component, verify Error 102 does not return, no unintended motion occurs, all applicable controls operate normally, each movement stops when released, and the bed is safe for clinical use.

CCR.Complaint: Stryker S3 hospital bed displayed Error 102 Call Service / Stuck Safety Relay. Staff reported concern for unreliable bed movement. Error was confirmed during normal operation after approximately one minute without a motion button being pressed.
CCR.Cause: Inspection found no physically stuck footboard, siderail, or pendant motion button and no visible external cable, connector, contamination, or power-related issue. Error remained active, indicating likely failure within the safety-relay or motion-control electronics path.
CCR.Resolution: Removed bed from patient service and labeled Out of Service due to unresolved motion-control error. Forwarded unit for bench evaluation and component replacement as indicated. Bed must pass complete motion-function verification before return to clinical use.

title: Stryker S3 Hospital Bed - Error: 301 Head Left Siderail Switch
description: Troubleshooting Error 301 Call Service, indicating unreliable head-left siderail position detection that may affect iBED Awareness siderail-status monitoring and patient fall-risk precautions.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Remove the bed from patient use if head-left siderail status or locking cannot be trusted. Transfer the patient to a known-working bed or establish approved fall-prevention measures before evaluation. Do not rely on iBED Awareness siderail-status indication while Error 301 is active.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Associated Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm Error 301 Call Service is displayed. Determine whether it appears at startup, during head-left siderail movement, during iBED Awareness setup or monitoring, or intermittently during bed handling. Observe whether the bed recognizes raised and lowered siderail positions.

steps.title: Check Power and General Bed Condition
steps.instructions: Confirm normal power from a known-working outlet and inspect for additional alarms, indicator abnormalities, damage, liquid contamination, or evidence of impact near the head-left siderail area.

steps.title: Physically Verify the Head-Left Siderail Position and Locking
steps.instructions: Raise and lower the head-left siderail manually. Confirm smooth travel, full raised and lowered positioning, secure locking when raised, normal release when lowered, and absence of looseness, bending, cracking, obstruction, or misalignment.

steps.title: Compare Physical Position to iBED Awareness Indication
steps.instructions: With the bed unloaded and removed from patient use, operate the head-left siderail between raised and lowered positions several times and observe whether iBED Awareness status accurately follows the actual physical siderail position.

steps.title: Inspect the Head-Left Siderail Switch Area and External Wiring Path
steps.instructions: Inspect accessible switch-area components and external wiring for loose connections, disconnection, pinched or damaged wiring, improper routing, debris, contamination, misalignment, impact damage, or excessive wear affecting reliable switch actuation.

steps.title: Correct an Identified External Connection or Obstruction Issue
steps.instructions: Correct any accessible loose connection, improper cable routing, or visible external obstruction according to approved Clinical Engineering practice. Then verify repeated siderail movement, secure locking, cleared Error 301 status, and correct iBED Awareness indication.

steps.title: Isolate a Likely Switch or Wiring Failure
steps.instructions: If the siderail operates mechanically but Error 301 remains, suspect the head-left siderail switch assembly, associated wiring, connector integrity, or actuation alignment. If locking is unreliable or damage is present, keep the bed out of service for repair.

CCR.Complaint: Stryker S3 bed displayed Error 301 Call Service. Staff reported the iBED Awareness system did not reliably indicate the actual position of the head-left siderail.
CCR.Cause: Head-left siderail mechanically raised and lowered, but iBED Awareness did not consistently recognize position changes. Accessible inspection identified a suspected head-left siderail switch or associated wiring/connection fault.
CCR.Resolution: Removed bed from service due to unresolved Error 301 and unreliable siderail-status indication. Labeled unit Out of Service and forwarded for repair of the head-left siderail switch circuit, followed by iBED Awareness functional verification.

title: Stryker S3 Hospital Bed - Error: 302 Head Right Siderail Switch
description: Troubleshooting Error 302 Call Service caused by a head-right siderail switch fault affecting reliable iBED Awareness siderail status monitoring.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Remove the bed from patient use when Error 302 Call Service is active and iBED Awareness status cannot be trusted. Transfer the patient to a known-working bed before troubleshooting, and do not rely on iBED Awareness indicators until the fault is corrected and verified.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Bed Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm that the display reports Error 302 Call Service. Document whether the error occurs at startup, during head-right siderail movement, intermittently, or continuously, and observe whether iBED Awareness correctly reflects raised and lowered positions.

steps.title: Confirm the Head-Right Siderail Is Physically Secure
steps.instructions: Raise and lower the head-right siderail through its normal range of motion. Confirm that it moves freely, fully raises, locks securely, releases normally, and is not obstructed by bedding, accessories, damage, or contamination.

steps.title: Check for External Damage or Contamination
steps.instructions: Inspect the head-right siderail area for cracked components, loose covers, contamination, debris, impact damage, or visibly damaged wiring where accessible without disassembly. Clean external contamination according to approved procedures and retest.

steps.title: Check Siderail Switch Actuation Behavior
steps.instructions: Move the head-right siderail between fully raised and fully lowered positions while observing bed recognition and iBED Awareness indication. Determine whether abnormal behavior occurs in either position, during movement, or intermittently.

steps.title: Inspect Accessible Wiring and Connections
steps.instructions: Following appropriate safety precautions, inspect only accessible head-right siderail switch wiring and connectors for looseness, damage, corrosion, fluid intrusion, or movement-related wear. Reseat accessible connections when appropriate and retest. Do not perform internal disassembly at the bedside.

steps.title: Correct the Identified External Cause and Verify Operation
steps.instructions: Correct any confirmed external obstruction, contamination issue, loose accessible connection, or visible actuation concern according to approved service practices. Verify repeated siderail operation, secure locking, cleared Error 302 status, correct iBED Awareness indication, and required functional and safety checks.

steps.title: Stop When Resolved
steps.instructions: When normal siderail-status monitoring has been restored and Error 302 no longer appears, document the findings and return the bed to service only after required verification. Do not continue troubleshooting once reliable operation is confirmed.

CCR.Complaint: Stryker S3 hospital bed displayed Error 302 Call Service. Staff reported iBED Awareness could not be relied upon to indicate the correct position of the head-right siderail.
CCR.Cause: Evaluation found unreliable head-right siderail position recognition due to a loose accessible siderail switch connection, preventing consistent raised/lowered status indication.
CCR.Resolution: Removed bed from service, inspected head-right siderail operation and accessible switch wiring, reseated the loose connector, and retested repeated siderail movement. Error 302 cleared, iBED Awareness correctly indicated head-right siderail position, and the bed passed functional verification before return to service.

title: Stryker S3 Hospital Bed - Error: 303 Foot Left Siderail Switch
description: Troubleshooting Error 303 indicating a foot-left siderail switch fault that can make iBED Awareness siderail status unreliable.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Remove the bed from patient use when dependable iBED Awareness siderail monitoring is required. Move the patient to a known-working bed before troubleshooting and do not rely on iBED Awareness to confirm the foot-left siderail position while the error is present.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm Error 303 Call Service is displayed and document whether it occurs at startup, when iBED Awareness is enabled, during foot-left siderail movement, or intermittently. Confirm whether the siderail raises, lowers, and locks mechanically.

steps.title: Confirm the Foot-Left Siderail Is Mechanically Secure
steps.instructions: With the bed unoccupied, raise and lower the foot-left siderail through its normal travel. Verify smooth movement, proper locking, normal release, and absence of damage or misalignment.

steps.title: Check Whether iBED Awareness Responds to Siderail Position
steps.instructions: Observe iBED Awareness indication while repeatedly raising and lowering the foot-left siderail. Compare the displayed status to the actual physical position.

steps.title: Inspect for Visible Switch Assembly or Wiring Problems
steps.instructions: Inspect the accessible foot-left siderail switch area and related cabling for visible damage, loose accessible connections, pinched or abraded wiring, debris, or poor mechanical actuation. Do not perform unnecessary internal disassembly.

steps.title: Correct Simple External or Accessible Findings
steps.instructions: Reseat an accessible loose connector according to facility repair practices, remove visible obstructions affecting movement, and retest. Stop troubleshooting and escalate for repair if wiring is visibly damaged or unsafe.

steps.title: Verify Resolution Before Returning the Bed to Service
steps.instructions: Verify foot-left siderail movement and locking, correct iBED Awareness recognition of position changes, absence of Error 303 after repeated operation, and completion of required facility safety checks before release.

CCR.Complaint: Stryker S3 hospital bed displays Error 303 Call Service. iBED Awareness foot-left siderail status may not reliably match the physical siderail position.
CCR.Cause: Foot-left siderail moved and locked mechanically, but iBED Awareness status did not consistently respond to siderail position changes. Accessible wiring and connections were inspected; fault remained, indicating likely failed switch assembly or associated wiring.
CCR.Resolution: Removed bed from service and labeled Out of Service due to unreliable iBED Awareness siderail monitoring. Sent for repair or bench evaluation of the foot-left siderail switch assembly and related wiring, with functional verification required before return to service.

title: Stryker S3 Hospital Bed - Error: 304 Foot Right Siderail Switch
description: Troubleshooting Error 304 when the foot-right siderail switch does not reliably report rail position to the iBED Awareness system, making siderail-status monitoring unreliable.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Remove the bed from patient use when Error 304 is active and siderail monitoring cannot be trusted. If occupied, notify clinical staff, manually confirm siderail position and locking, transfer the patient to another appropriate bed when reliable monitoring is required, and do not rely on iBED Awareness while the error remains active.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Error and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm that the bed displays or logs Error 304 Call Service. Document whether it occurs at power-up, during siderail movement, at the locked position, or intermittently. With the bed removed from patient use, verify whether the foot-right siderail moves and locks normally.

steps.title: Manually Confirm Foot-Right Siderail Position and Locking
steps.instructions: Raise and lower the foot-right siderail through its normal range of travel. Confirm smooth movement, full positioning, secure locking when raised, proper release when lowered, and absence of looseness, misalignment, binding, or obstruction.

steps.title: Inspect for Obstructions, Damage, or Misalignment
steps.instructions: Inspect for debris, contamination, damaged siderail components, misalignment, impact damage, or incomplete seating. Correct simple external obstructions or obvious positioning issues that can be safely addressed without disassembly.

steps.title: Inspect the Foot-Right Siderail Switch Area
steps.instructions: Visually inspect the accessible foot-right siderail switch area and mechanical engagement point for visible damage, loose mounting, wear, contamination, or inconsistent actuation during siderail movement.

steps.title: Check Accessible Harness Routing and Connector Seating
steps.instructions: Inspect accessible wiring for loose connectors, pinching, cuts, abrasion, strain, improper routing, corrosion, or contamination. Reseat accessible connectors as appropriate and ensure harness routing does not interfere with siderail movement.

steps.title: Recheck the Error After Correcting External Conditions
steps.instructions: After correcting any external obstruction, loose connection, or harness routing issue, cycle the foot-right siderail several times. Confirm that Error 304 no longer returns and that iBED Awareness accurately identifies both raised and lowered siderail positions.

steps.title: Isolate a Likely Switch or Wiring Failure
steps.instructions: If Error 304 persists after external checks and the siderail moves and locks normally, suspect a failed or intermittent foot-right siderail switch, associated wiring fault, connector damage, or mechanical engagement issue requiring repair evaluation.

CCR.Complaint: Stryker S3 hospital bed displayed Error 304 Call Service for the foot-right siderail switch. Staff reported iBED Awareness was not reliably confirming foot-right siderail position.
CCR.Cause: Inspection identified a loose foot-right siderail switch connector causing intermittent siderail-position detection. Siderail movement and mechanical locking were normal.
CCR.Resolution: Removed bed from patient use, reseated and secured the accessible foot-right siderail switch connection, verified harness routing, cycled the siderail repeatedly, and confirmed iBED Awareness correctly detected raised and lowered siderail positions. Bed returned to service after functional verification.

title: Stryker LUCAS 3 Mechanical CPR Device - Battery Will Not Charge / Short Runtime
description: Troubleshooting LUCAS 3 battery charging failure, short runtime, charger issues, battery seating problems, or battery condition concerns.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: If the LUCAS 3 is in use or staged for an active resuscitation response, do not troubleshoot the device on a patient or during a code. Remove the device from clinical use and replace it with another ready LUCAS 3 or approved manual CPR backup process. Expected outcome: Patient care is not dependent on a device with uncertain battery performance.

steps.title: Confirm the Reported Battery Problem
steps.instructions: Verify the complaint with clinical staff. Determine whether the issue is: Battery will not charge; Battery runtime is short; Device shuts down on battery; Battery indicator drops quickly; Battery does not show charged after being on charger; Device only works on external power. Expected outcome: The failure mode is clearly identified before testing.

steps.title: Inspect the Battery Externally
steps.instructions: Remove the battery and inspect it for: Cracked housing; Swelling; Damaged contacts; Contamination or fluid exposure; Loose fit in the device or charger; Heat, odor, or discoloration. Do not continue using a battery with physical damage, swelling, overheating, or suspected fluid intrusion. Expected outcome: The battery is physically safe to handle and test.

steps.title: Verify Battery Seating in the LUCAS 3
steps.instructions: Reinsert the battery fully into the LUCAS 3 and confirm it latches securely. Power the device on and check whether the battery status displays normally. Expected outcome: The battery is recognized and the device powers normally from battery power. If reseating resolves the issue, document the battery seating issue and stop.

steps.title: Check the Battery Contacts
steps.instructions: Inspect the battery contacts and device battery compartment contacts for visible debris, corrosion, bent contacts, or residue. Clean only according to facility-approved cleaning practices and manufacturer-compatible methods. Do not scrape, bend, or modify the contacts. Expected outcome: Contacts are clean, dry, and undamaged.

steps.title: Test With a Known-Good Battery
steps.instructions: Install a known-good charged LUCAS 3 battery into the device. Power the device on and observe whether it starts normally and maintains operation. Expected outcome: The device operates normally with a known-good battery. If the device works normally with another battery, the original battery is likely the issue and should be removed from circulation.

steps.title: Test the Suspect Battery in a Known-Good Charger
steps.instructions: Place the suspect battery into a known-good compatible LUCAS battery charger. Confirm that the battery seats properly and the charger indicates normal charging behavior. Expected outcome: The charger recognizes the battery and charging begins. If the charger does not recognize the battery, or charging fails repeatedly, remove the battery from service.

steps.title: Check the Charger and Power Source
steps.instructions: Verify the charger is connected to a working outlet. Check for: Secure power cord connection; Charger indicator lights; Damaged charger housing; Damaged cord or plug; Unusual heat, smell, or noise. Test the outlet if needed, or move the charger to a verified outlet. Expected outcome: The charger has reliable AC power and normal indicator behavior.

steps.title: Try a Known-Good Battery on the Same Charger
steps.instructions: Place a known-good LUCAS 3 battery into the same charger. Expected outcome: The known-good battery charges normally. If no batteries charge in that charger, suspect the charger, power cord, outlet, or charger power supply instead of the battery.

steps.title: Verify Charging Time and Battery Rotation Practices
steps.instructions: Ask whether the battery was allowed to charge fully and whether batteries are being rotated regularly. Short runtime can occur if batteries are repeatedly placed into service before completing a full charge cycle. Expected outcome: The battery has had adequate time on a working charger before being judged as failed.

steps.title: Check Battery Age and Service History
steps.instructions: Review the battery asset history, purchase date, service notes, and prior runtime complaints. Batteries used in emergency response devices should not remain in service if they show repeated short runtime, intermittent charging, or unreliable charge indication. Expected outcome: Battery condition is evaluated based on both current test results and history.

steps.title: Perform a Controlled Runtime Check if Safe and Allowed
steps.instructions: In a bench setting only, install a fully charged suspect battery and operate the LUCAS 3 according to facility test practice. Monitor for: Rapid battery indicator drop; Unexpected shutdown; Battery alarm or warning; Excessive heat; Intermittent power loss. Expected outcome: The battery supports expected operation without abnormal shutdown or rapid depletion. If short runtime is confirmed, remove the battery from service.

steps.title: Check External Power Operation
steps.instructions: If available and appropriate for your facility workflow, verify whether the LUCAS 3 operates normally using the approved external power supply. Expected outcome: The device operates normally on external power. If the device fails on both battery and external power, the issue is more likely device-related and not isolated to the battery.

steps.title: Do Not Attempt Internal Battery Repair
steps.instructions: Do not open, rebuild, bypass, or modify the LUCAS 3 battery pack. Do not attempt to use damaged lithium-ion batteries. Expected outcome: Battery safety is maintained and unsafe battery handling is avoided.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported that the Stryker LUCAS 3 battery would not hold a charge and the device showed short runtime during readiness check.
CCR.Cause: Battery was recognized by the device but showed rapid depletion after full charging; known-good battery operated normally in the same LUCAS 3.
CCR.Resolution: Removed the suspect battery from service, verified the LUCAS 3 operated normally with a known-good charged battery, checked charger operation, and returned the device to service with a good battery.

helpfulDetails: Battery serial number or asset ID if tracked
Whether the battery charged in a known-good charger
Whether a known-good battery worked in the device
Outlet tested or charger moved to known-good outlet
Battery age or prior runtime complaints
Any swelling, heat, odor, damage, or contamination
Whether device operated on external power

title: Stryker LUCAS 3 Mechanical CPR Device - Device Will Not Power On Or Fails Startup Self-Test
description: Troubleshooting LUCAS 3 power, battery, connection, and startup self-test issues before escalating for repair.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions:
If the LUCAS 3 is in use or being prepared for patient use and does not power on or fails startup, remove it from clinical use immediately.

Use another verified mechanical CPR device or continue manual CPR according to clinical protocol.

Expected outcome: Patient care is not delayed or dependent on a device that cannot complete startup.

Why it matters: A mechanical CPR device must power on, initialize, and pass startup checks before it can be trusted for patient care.

steps.title: Confirm the Reported Failure
steps.instructions:
Attempt to power on the LUCAS 3 in a controlled Clinical Engineering setting.

Observe whether the device:

Does not respond at all
Powers briefly and shuts down
Displays a battery or power indicator issue
Starts but fails self-test
Produces an alarm, warning tone, or fault indication

Expected outcome: The failure mode is confirmed before parts or repair decisions are made.

If the device powers on normally and passes startup repeatedly, document “could not duplicate,” inspect the device, and return to service only if all checks are acceptable.

steps.title: Check for Obvious External Damage
steps.instructions:
Inspect the LUCAS 3 for signs of impact, liquid intrusion, cracked housing, damaged control panel, missing parts, or contamination.

Check the compression piston area, straps, support legs, back plate interface, and battery compartment.

Expected outcome: No physical condition is present that would prevent safe startup.

If damage, fluid intrusion, unusual odor, heat, or contamination is found, stop troubleshooting and remove the device from service.

steps.title: Verify Battery Installation
steps.instructions:
Remove and reinstall the battery, confirming it seats fully and latches properly.

Inspect the battery contacts and battery compartment contacts for debris, corrosion, bent pins, contamination, or visible damage.

Expected outcome: The battery is fully seated and the device responds when powered on.

If reseating the battery resolves the issue and the device passes startup, perform a full functional check before returning it to service.

steps.title: Try a Known-Good Battery
steps.instructions:
Install a known-good, charged LUCAS 3 battery from another verified device or battery inventory.

Power the unit on and observe startup behavior.

Expected outcome: The device powers on and completes startup with the known-good battery.

If the device works with a known-good battery, suspect the original battery is discharged, failed, or unable to support load. Remove the questionable battery from service and document the result.

steps.title: Check Battery Charge Status
steps.instructions:
Place the suspect battery on the approved charger and observe charger indicators.

Confirm whether the charger recognizes the battery, charges normally, or reports a fault.

Expected outcome: The battery charges normally and can power the device after charging.

If the battery will not charge, shows abnormal charger behavior, or provides short runtime after charging, remove the battery from service.

steps.title: Verify External Power and Charger Source
steps.instructions:
Confirm the charger or power supply is connected to a known-good outlet.

Test the outlet or plug the charger into another verified outlet.

Inspect the power cord, charger, and connectors for damage or loose fit.

Expected outcome: The power source and charging equipment are not the cause of the battery or startup complaint.

If the charger or cord is faulty, replace or remove it from service and retest the device with a known-good charged battery.

steps.title: Check the Power Button and Control Panel Response
steps.instructions:
Press the power button normally and observe for indicator lights, display response, sounds, or motor initialization.

Do not repeatedly force the button or attempt to bypass the control panel.

Expected outcome: The device responds consistently to the power command.

If the button feels stuck, damaged, intermittent, or produces no response with a known-good battery, suspect a control panel, internal power path, or electronic fault.

steps.title: Observe Startup Self-Test Behavior
steps.instructions:
If the LUCAS 3 powers on but fails startup self-test, note exactly what happens.

Document:

Audible alarm or tone behavior
Indicator lights or display messages
Whether the piston moves or initializes
Whether the device shuts down
Whether the failure is repeatable
Whether the issue occurs with multiple known-good batteries

Expected outcome: Startup failure is characterized clearly for repair evaluation.

If the failure repeats with known-good power and no external obstruction, the unit should not be used clinically.

steps.title: Inspect for External Obstruction or Mechanical Binding
steps.instructions:
With the device off and removed from patient use, visually inspect the piston and external moving components for obvious obstruction, debris, strap entanglement, or physical damage.

Do not disassemble the compression mechanism.

Expected outcome: No external condition is preventing normal initialization.

If an external obstruction is found and safely cleared, restart the device and confirm it passes startup. If the issue resolves, complete a full function check before returning to service.

steps.title: Check for Environmental or Cleaning-Related Issues
steps.instructions:
Ask whether the device was recently cleaned, exposed to fluids, dropped, stored in a cold or hot area, or used during a transport event.

Look for moisture near the battery bay, control area, connectors, and housing seams.

Expected outcome: No recent event suggests contamination or internal damage.

If fluid exposure or impact is suspected, remove the device from service even if it powers on intermittently.

steps.title: Perform a Controlled Restart
steps.instructions:
Remove the battery, wait briefly, reinstall a known-good charged battery, and power the device on again.

Expected outcome: Temporary startup lockup clears and the device completes self-test.

If the device powers on and passes startup repeatedly, continue with facility-required operational testing before returning to service.

steps.title: Determine Whether the Issue Is Battery-Related or Device-Related
steps.instructions:
Compare results:

Original battery fails, known-good battery works: battery issue
Multiple known-good batteries fail: device issue
Device fails only after movement or handling: possible intermittent connection or internal fault
Device powers on but fails self-test every time: internal electronic, control, or drive system issue likely

Expected outcome: Troubleshooting identifies whether to remove the battery, charger, or full device from service.

steps.title: Stop if Safe Operation Cannot Be Verified
steps.instructions:
If the LUCAS 3 does not power on reliably, fails startup self-test repeatedly, shuts down unexpectedly, or shows signs of damage, remove it from service.

Expected outcome: The device is not returned to patient care unless startup and operation are dependable.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported that the Stryker LUCAS 3 would not power on during pre-use check and failed to complete startup.
CCR.Cause: Verified failure with the installed battery; device powered on normally with a known-good charged battery, indicating the original battery was unable to support operation.
CCR.Resolution: Removed the failed battery from service, tested the LUCAS 3 with a known-good battery, confirmed successful startup, and returned the device to service after functional verification.

helpfulDetails: Signs of impact or fluid exposure

title: Stryker LUCAS 3 Mechanical CPR Device - Suction Cup / Piston Positioning Alarm
description: Troubleshooting suction cup, piston, or patient positioning alarms caused by setup, obstruction, attachment, or movement issues.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: If the LUCAS 3 is being used during patient care and a suction cup or piston positioning alarm occurs, immediately follow facility resuscitation protocol. Have clinical staff resume manual compressions or move to another verified mechanical CPR device if available. Expected outcome: Chest compressions continue without unsafe interruption. Why it matters: A positioning alarm may indicate the device cannot deliver compressions at the correct depth or location.

steps.title: Do Not Troubleshoot on an Active Patient Unless Clinically Safe
steps.instructions: Clinical Engineering should not adjust, test, or repeatedly restart the device on an active patient unless directed by the code team and it is safe to do so. Expected outcome: Troubleshooting does not delay effective CPR. If the device cannot be quickly corrected during use, remove it from patient service and document the failure.

steps.title: Confirm the Reported Alarm or Symptom
steps.instructions: In a controlled setting, power on the LUCAS 3 and confirm the reported issue. Look for symptoms such as: Suction cup positioning alarm; Piston not lowering correctly; Piston stopping before reaching the chest; Device requesting repositioning; Compression start failure; Alarm after patient movement or transport. Expected outcome: The reported alarm is confirmed or the issue cannot be duplicated.

steps.title: Inspect the Suction Cup Condition
steps.instructions: Check the suction cup for: Tears; Deformation; Hardening; Loose attachment; Contamination; Missing or incorrect suction cup; Improper seating on the piston. Expected outcome: The suction cup is intact, flexible, clean, and properly attached. If the suction cup is damaged, replace it with the correct approved part if available, then retest. If this resolves the alarm, stop.

steps.title: Verify the Piston Moves Freely Without Obstruction
steps.instructions: With the device off and not on a patient, visually inspect the piston area. Check for: Foreign material around the piston; Dried fluids or contamination; Cracked or damaged external components; Binding or abnormal resistance; Obvious mechanical damage from a drop or impact. Expected outcome: The piston path is clean and unobstructed. Do not force the piston or disassemble the drive mechanism.

steps.title: Check for Improper Device Positioning
steps.instructions: Review how the device was placed when the alarm occurred. Confirm: Back plate was correctly positioned under the patient; Upper unit was locked evenly onto the back plate; Suction cup was centered over the correct compression point; Patient was not shifted, angled, or partially off the back plate; Device was not tilted or twisted during transport. Expected outcome: The device is positioned squarely and centered before compression begins. Why it matters: If the frame is misaligned, the piston may not detect or contact the chest properly.

steps.title: Inspect the Back Plate and Locking Claws
steps.instructions: Check the back plate and upper unit attachment points for: Cracks; Bent locking areas; Broken latch components; Dirt or debris preventing full engagement; Uneven locking between sides. Expected outcome: Both sides lock securely and evenly with no visible damage. If the upper unit does not lock securely to the back plate, remove the device from service.

steps.title: Check Patient Size and Chest Positioning Factors
steps.instructions: Review whether the patient condition may have contributed to the alarm. Possible external factors include: Very small or very large chest size; Patient not flat on a firm surface; Excessive clothing, pads, or equipment under the suction cup; Patient movement during transfer; Device placed over defibrillator pads, dressings, or lines. Expected outcome: The compression site is clear and the patient setup allows correct piston positioning.

steps.title: Inspect for Contamination After Clinical Use
steps.instructions: After cleaning according to facility procedure, inspect around the suction cup and piston area again. Look for dried blood, gel, adhesive residue, vomit, or cleaning residue that could affect piston travel or suction cup seating. Expected outcome: External surfaces are clean and dry, with no residue interfering with operation.

steps.title: Verify Battery and Startup Status
steps.instructions: Install a known-good charged battery and power the device on. Confirm the device completes startup without unrelated alarms. Expected outcome: The LUCAS 3 powers on normally and does not show battery, service, or self-test faults. Why it matters: Low power or startup faults may be mistaken for a positioning problem during a code.

steps.title: Perform a Controlled Functional Check
steps.instructions: In a safe bench or training setting, use the approved test method, training manikin, or facility-approved verification process. Confirm: Piston lowers appropriately; Suction cup contacts the test surface correctly; Device transitions through setup without positioning alarms; No abnormal noise, hesitation, or binding occurs; Compression function starts and stops as expected. Expected outcome: The device operates normally without a suction cup or piston positioning alarm. If the alarm clears after correcting setup, cleaning, or suction cup condition, document the finding and return the device only after successful functional verification.

steps.title: Evaluate for Drop or Transport Damage
steps.instructions: Ask clinical staff whether the device was dropped, struck, transported roughly, or removed quickly during a code. Inspect the frame, piston area, locking points, and back plate for visible damage. Expected outcome: No external damage is present. If damage is found or suspected, remove the device from service even if it powers on.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported the Stryker LUCAS 3 displayed a suction cup positioning alarm and would not begin compressions during setup.
CCR.Cause: Inspection found the suction cup was partially detached from the piston and not seating evenly during the setup check.
CCR.Resolution: Reinstalled the suction cup correctly, verified the back plate and locking arms, completed a functional check without alarm, and returned the device to service.

helpfulDetails: Whether alarm occurred during setup or active compression
Whether patient was moved or transported
Any abnormal sounds, hesitation, binding, heat, or odor
Whether contamination or residue was found

title: Stryker LUCAS 3 Mechanical CPR Device - Compression Stops, Weak Compression, Or Drive Mechanism Fault
description: Troubleshooting interrupted, weak, or abnormal LUCAS 3 compression performance before escalating for repair.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions:
If the LUCAS 3 stops compressing, compresses weakly, or shows a drive-related fault during patient use, clinical staff must immediately resume manual CPR according to facility protocol.

Do not continue relying on the device if compression depth, rhythm, or piston movement appears unreliable.

Expected outcome: Patient circulation support is maintained without depending on a questionable mechanical CPR device.

steps.title: Remove the Device From Active Use When Safe
steps.instructions:
Once patient care has been transferred to manual CPR or another approved method, remove the LUCAS 3 from the patient area for Clinical Engineering evaluation.

Expected outcome: Troubleshooting is performed away from the active patient care event.

If the issue occurred during an active code, document the reported behavior clearly.

steps.title: Confirm the Reported Symptom
steps.instructions:
Power the LUCAS 3 on and observe the startup behavior.

Check whether the issue is:

Compression stops during operation
Weak or shallow piston movement
Failure to start compressions
Drive mechanism fault
Abnormal motor sound
Intermittent operation when moved or handled

Expected outcome: The reported failure is confirmed or identified as intermittent.

steps.title: Check Battery Charge and Seating
steps.instructions:
Remove and reinstall the battery, ensuring it is fully seated and latched.

Check the battery charge indicator.

If available, test with a known-good charged LUCAS 3 battery.

Expected outcome: The device powers normally and runs without compression interruption.

If battery replacement resolves the issue, remove the suspect battery from service and stop troubleshooting the device.

steps.title: Check External Power Supply and Charging Accessories
steps.instructions:
Inspect the external power supply, power cord, charger, and battery charger contacts for damage, looseness, contamination, or missing components.

Verify that the battery charges normally in the approved charger or through the device if applicable.

Expected outcome: Power accessories are ruled out as the cause of low power or unexpected shutdown.

steps.title: Inspect the Device for Physical Damage
steps.instructions:
Look for cracks, impact marks, bent components, loose hardware, broken hooks, damaged legs, or signs that the device was dropped.

Pay close attention to the upper housing, support legs, back plate connection points, and piston area.

Expected outcome: No physical damage is present that could affect compression alignment or drive movement.

If damage is found, remove the device from service and send it for repair or manufacturer evaluation.

steps.title: Verify Correct Assembly With the Back Plate
steps.instructions:
Attach the LUCAS 3 to its back plate and confirm both support legs lock securely.

Check for poor latching, uneven engagement, or movement between the upper unit and back plate.

Expected outcome: The upper unit attaches firmly and remains stable.

Why it matters: Poor mechanical alignment can affect compression position, force transfer, and device stability.

steps.title: Inspect the Suction Cup and Piston Area
steps.instructions:
Check the suction cup for tears, deformation, improper attachment, contamination, or stiffness.

Inspect the piston area externally for debris, fluid residue, dried cleaning agent, or obstruction.

Expected outcome: The suction cup and piston area are clean, intact, and able to move without visible restriction.

If the suction cup is damaged or worn, replace it according to facility policy and retest.

steps.title: Check for Obvious Obstruction or Binding
steps.instructions:
With the device off and removed from any patient use, visually inspect for anything preventing normal piston travel.

Do not force the piston, open the housing, or disassemble the drive mechanism.

Expected outcome: No external obstruction is present.

If binding, grinding, or restricted movement is suspected, stop troubleshooting and escalate.

steps.title: Run a Controlled Functional Check
steps.instructions:
In a safe bench setting, power the device on and initiate a functional test according to facility procedure.

Observe compression startup, piston motion, sound, alerts, and whether the device stops unexpectedly.

Expected outcome: Compression motion is consistent, strong, and free of abnormal noise or fault indicators.

If the device completes the check normally, document the result and consider whether the original issue may have been related to battery charge, setup, patient positioning, or accessory condition.

steps.title: Listen for Abnormal Drive Sounds
steps.instructions:
During testing, listen for grinding, clicking, straining, slipping, rattling, or sudden motor speed changes.

Expected outcome: The motor and drive sound smooth and consistent.

If abnormal sounds are present, remove the device from service. This may indicate an internal drive, motor, gear, or compression mechanism issue.

steps.title: Check for Heat, Odor, or Electrical Warning Signs
steps.instructions:
Inspect the housing and battery area for unusual heat, burning odor, melted plastic, or discoloration.

Expected outcome: No heat, odor, or electrical damage is present.

If any of these are found, stop testing immediately and label the device Out of Service.

steps.title: Review Error Indicators or Device Logs if Available
steps.instructions:
Check displayed alarms, indicators, or stored event/service information according to approved Clinical Engineering workflow.

Note any recurring drive, compression, battery, motor, or service-related faults.

Expected outcome: Fault information supports the observed symptom and helps determine whether repair escalation is needed.

steps.title: Retest With Known-Good External Components
steps.instructions:
If the device behavior is intermittent, retest using:

Known-good charged battery
Known-good suction cup
Known-good back plate if available
Known-good power supply or charger if charging is part of the complaint

Expected outcome: The issue either follows an accessory or remains with the device.

If the issue follows an accessory, remove that accessory from service. If the issue remains with the device, escalate for repair.

steps.title: Return to Service Only if Fully Verified
steps.instructions:
Return the LUCAS 3 to service only if it passes operational checks, has no active faults, shows normal compression operation, and has no signs of mechanical damage.

Expected outcome: The device is confirmed safe and ready for emergency use.

If there is any doubt about compression strength or drive reliability, do not return it to service.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported that the Stryker LUCAS 3 stopped compressions during use and displayed a drive-related fault.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering verified normal battery seating and accessory condition, but the device produced intermittent compression stoppage and abnormal drive noise during bench testing.
CCR.Resolution: LUCAS 3 was removed from service, labeled Out of Service, and sent for repair evaluation due to suspected internal drive mechanism fault.

helpfulDetails: External power supply or charger tested
Piston area inspected for debris or obstruction
Compression behavior observed during bench test
Abnormal motor or drive noise noted
Unusual heat, smell, or housing damage checked

title: Stryker LUCAS 3 Mechanical CPR Device - Wi-Fi / LIFENET / Post-Event Data Transfer Failure
description: Troubleshooting LUCAS 3 Wi-Fi, LIFENET, or post-event data transfer issues caused by power, configuration, network, or workflow problems.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Confirm the LUCAS 3 is not being troubleshot during active patient use. If the device is needed for a code or transport, place another verified LUCAS 3 or approved manual CPR backup process in service first. Expected outcome: Troubleshooting is performed only when the device is not required for active resuscitation.

steps.title: Confirm the Complaint and Transfer Method
steps.instructions: Ask clinical staff what failed: Wi-Fi connection; LIFENET communication; Post-event data upload; Event file retrieval; Device not appearing in the receiving system; Transfer works intermittently. Expected outcome: The issue is narrowed to network connection, destination system communication, or post-event data handling.

steps.title: Verify the Device Powers On Normally
steps.instructions: Install a charged LUCAS 3 battery and power the device on. Confirm the device completes startup without fault indicators or abnormal alarms. Expected outcome: The LUCAS 3 powers on normally before communication troubleshooting continues. If the device fails startup, resolve the power or device fault first.

steps.title: Check Battery Charge Level
steps.instructions: Confirm the installed battery has adequate charge. If the battery is low, install a known-good charged battery or place the battery on the approved charger. Expected outcome: Data transfer is attempted with reliable power available. Why it matters: Communication attempts can fail or be interrupted if the device shuts down or enters a low-power condition.

steps.title: Confirm the Event Data Exists
steps.instructions: Verify there was an actual recent device use or test event expected to generate data. Confirm staff are not expecting an upload from a device that was powered on but not used long enough to create meaningful event data. Expected outcome: The reported missing transfer is tied to a real event or stored record.

steps.title: Check Device Date and Time
steps.instructions: Review the LUCAS 3 date and time setting if accessible through the facility’s normal configuration workflow. Expected outcome: Event records are not being misfiled because of an incorrect timestamp. Why it matters: Incorrect date or time can make a successful upload appear missing in the receiving system.

steps.title: Verify Wi-Fi Is Enabled and Configured
steps.instructions: Confirm the device is configured for the facility’s intended wireless network and post-event transfer workflow. Check for obvious configuration concerns such as: Wrong Wi-Fi profile; Incorrect network name; Recently changed password; Device not assigned to the correct organization or receiving account; Device replaced or reset without reconfiguration. Expected outcome: The LUCAS 3 is configured for the correct wireless and data destination environment.

steps.title: Confirm Network Availability at the Device Location
steps.instructions: Test the transfer in an area known to have reliable facility Wi-Fi coverage. Avoid testing in dead zones such as elevators, ambulance bays, stairwells, basements, storage rooms, or shielded areas. Expected outcome: The device can attempt communication in an area with adequate wireless signal.

steps.title: Check for Recent IT or Network Changes
steps.instructions: Ask whether there were recent changes involving: Wi-Fi password; SSID; Firewall rules; Certificate requirements; Device network access lists; LIFENET gateway or account settings. Expected outcome: Facility-side changes are identified before assuming the LUCAS 3 has failed.

steps.title: Compare With Another LUCAS 3
steps.instructions: If another LUCAS 3 is available, attempt the same workflow from the same location. Expected outcome: If both devices fail, suspect network, LIFENET, account, or facility configuration. If only one device fails, suspect that device’s configuration, wireless module, or stored event handling.

steps.title: Verify the Device Identifier in the Receiving System
steps.instructions: Confirm the LUCAS 3 serial number or device identifier matches what LIFENET or the receiving platform expects. Expected outcome: The uploaded data is associated with the correct device record. Why it matters: Data may transfer successfully but appear under the wrong device, site, or account if identifiers are mismatched.

steps.title: Attempt a Controlled Data Transfer
steps.instructions: Perform a controlled post-event data transfer according to facility-approved workflow. Observe for: Transfer status messages; Failure prompts; No response; Repeated timeout; Successful transfer but missing record downstream. Expected outcome: The failure point is documented clearly. If the transfer completes successfully, return the device to service after confirming normal operation and documentation. Stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: Check LIFENET or Receiving Platform Access
steps.instructions: Confirm the receiving system is reachable and that authorized staff can view incoming events. Verify whether the issue is limited to one user account, one receiving site, or all users. Expected outcome: A login, permission, account, or cloud-side issue is ruled in or out.

steps.title: Inspect the Device Externally
steps.instructions: Inspect the LUCAS 3 for signs of damage that may affect operation or communication, including: Cracked housing; Fluid intrusion evidence; Missing covers; Damage from drop or transport; Unusual heat or smell; Corroded contacts or connectors. Expected outcome: No obvious physical damage is present. If damage or contamination is found, remove the device from service and send it for bench evaluation.

steps.title: Document Any Error Codes or Status Messages
steps.instructions: Record the exact communication message, transfer status, LIFENET response, or observed behavior. Expected outcome: The work order includes enough detail for IT, vendor support, or bench repair to reproduce the issue.

steps.title: Coordinate With IT Before Repair Escalation
steps.instructions: If Wi-Fi or LIFENET transfer still fails, confirm with IT that the device is allowed on the network and that required destination access is not blocked. Expected outcome: Network-side causes are ruled out before the device is sent for repair.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported that the Stryker LUCAS 3 would not upload post-event data to LIFENET after use.
CCR.Cause: Verified the device powered on normally and event data was present, but transfer failed on the facility Wi-Fi while another LUCAS 3 uploaded successfully from the same location.
CCR.Resolution: Removed the affected LUCAS 3 from service, labeled it Out of Service, documented the failed transfer behavior, and sent it for vendor/bench evaluation of communication function.

helpfulDetails: Battery charge level during transfer attempt
Whether the device powered on normally
Exact Wi-Fi or LIFENET error message
Date and time shown on the device
Device serial number or asset ID
Any recent network, password, or LIFENET account changes
Indicator lights, alarms, or status messages observed
Any physical damage, fluid exposure, heat, smell, or drop history
Final device status: returned to service, held for IT review, or removed from service

title: Stryker LIFEPAK 35 Defibrillator - Touchscreen Unresponsive / Frozen
description: Troubleshooting a frozen, delayed, or unresponsive touchscreen caused by contamination, environmental conditions, power state, software lockup, or hardware failure.

steps.title: 1. Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot an unresponsive touchscreen while the LIFEPAK 35 is supporting an active patient. If the touchscreen prevents reliable access to required monitoring, configuration, or therapy functions, immediately provide clinical staff with another verified defibrillator and remove the affected unit from patient use. Expected: Patient care continues with a known-good device. Why it matters: The LIFEPAK 35 touchscreen is a major user-interface component. Unreliable interface operation can affect safe and predictable device control. If transferring to another device resolves the immediate clinical concern, continue troubleshooting only in a controlled Clinical Engineering setting.

steps.title: 2. Verify the Exact Failure Behavior
steps.instructions: Power on the device and determine whether the touchscreen is: Completely unresponsive; Responsive only in certain screen areas; Responding intermittently; Responding slowly; Displaying normally but not accepting touch input; Frozen on one screen; Showing abnormal graphics, blank areas, or display corruption; Recovering after a delay without intervention. Also determine whether physical controls remain responsive. Expected: The failure pattern is clearly identified and reproducible. Why it matters: A total touchscreen failure, localized dead zone, and complete system freeze may indicate different fault paths.

steps.title: 3. Inspect the Touchscreen Surface
steps.instructions: Visually inspect the display for: Cracks; Impact damage; Deep scratches; Liquid contamination; Cleaning chemical residue; Heavy soil; Adhesive residue; Moisture around the screen perimeter; A screen protector or accessory interfering with operation. Clean the touchscreen only with methods and agents approved for the device. Allow the surface to dry fully before retesting. Expected: The screen is clean, dry, intact, and free of anything that could interfere with touch detection. If touchscreen operation returns to normal, document the contamination or residue found, complete required functional checks, and stop.

steps.title: 4. Remove External Sources of Unintended Touch Input
steps.instructions: Confirm that nothing is continuously contacting or pressing against the touchscreen, including: Cables; Carrying-case material; Straps; Mounted accessories; Packaging; Cleaning cloths; Other equipment. Place the LIFEPAK 35 on a stable surface and retest. Expected: The touchscreen responds normally without unintended external contact. If normal operation returns, correct the positioning or accessory interference and stop.

steps.title: 5. Check Environmental Conditions
steps.instructions: Determine whether the issue began after: Rapid movement between hot and cold environments; Visible condensation; Heavy moisture exposure; Recent cleaning; Storage in extreme temperature conditions; Significant impact or drop. Allow the device to stabilize in an appropriate operating environment before further testing when environmental exposure is suspected. Expected: The device is dry, environmentally stabilized, and the touchscreen responds consistently. If normal operation returns, document the environmental condition and complete functional verification before return to service.

steps.title: 6. Verify Power Condition
steps.instructions: Confirm the LIFEPAK 35 has a stable power source. Check: Battery installation; Battery charge indication; External power connection, when applicable; Power-related warnings or abnormal indicators; Whether the freeze occurs only on battery or only with external power. When available, test with a known-good compatible charged battery or verified power configuration. Expected: The device has stable power and the touchscreen remains responsive. If the issue disappears with a known-good power source, troubleshoot the battery or power-source problem separately and stop.

steps.title: 7. Perform a Controlled Restart
steps.instructions: With the device removed from patient use, perform a normal power-down and restart using the standard device controls. Do not repeatedly cycle power during active patient care. Observe: Whether shutdown completes normally; Whether startup completes normally; Whether the touchscreen responds immediately after startup; Whether the freeze returns after a specific function is opened; Whether any service indicator, warning, or error appears. Expected: The LIFEPAK 35 completes startup and the touchscreen remains responsive. If a single controlled restart restores operation, do not automatically assume the device is ready for service. Continue with repeated functional verification because an intermittent freeze on a defibrillator may recur.

steps.title: 8. Disconnect Nonessential External Accessories
steps.instructions: With the device safely out of clinical use, disconnect nonessential external accessories one at a time, as applicable, such as: USB-connected accessories; Data or communication connections; External peripheral interfaces; Nonessential monitoring accessories. Restart and retest after simplifying the configuration. Expected: The touchscreen remains responsive with the device in a basic configuration. If removing a specific external accessory consistently resolves the problem, inspect and isolate that accessory or connection before reconnecting it.

steps.title: 9. Check for Repeatable Trigger Conditions
steps.instructions: Operate the device through a controlled basic checkout and note whether the touchscreen freezes: Immediately at startup; After a specific menu opens; When a particular parameter is selected; During alarm interaction; During patient setup; After an accessory is connected; After prolonged operation; Only intermittently. Expected: Either no recurrence occurs or a repeatable trigger is identified. Why it matters: A repeatable trigger can help distinguish a general touch-input problem from a broader software, interface, or subsystem fault.

steps.title: 10. Review Device Status and Available Diagnostic Information
steps.instructions: Check for: Service indicator; Failed self-test; Readiness failure; Logged error condition; Repeated restart behavior; Other simultaneous control or display abnormalities. Record exact error wording or codes when available. Do not clear useful diagnostic evidence before documenting it. Expected: Any associated system fault is identified and preserved for repair evaluation.

steps.title: 11. Perform Required Functional Verification
steps.instructions: If the touchscreen appears restored, complete the organization’s approved LIFEPAK 35 operational checkout and applicable manufacturer-defined performance inspection before return to service. Stryker publishes a dedicated LIFEPAK 35 Performance Inspection Procedure for determining whether the device operates within required specifications. Verify at minimum that: Touch response is consistent across the usable interface; No obvious dead zones are present; Screen changes occur normally; Physical controls operate correctly; Startup completes normally; No service indication remains; Required monitoring and therapy-related checks pass according to approved procedures. Expected: The device passes required inspection without recurrence. If the screen freezes again, responds inconsistently, or fails any required check, stop troubleshooting and escalate.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported the LIFEPAK 35 touchscreen became frozen and would not respond to touch input during device setup.
CCR.Cause: Inspection found the touchscreen remained intermittently unresponsive after cleaning, power verification, controlled restart, and testing with nonessential external connections removed.
CCR.Resolution: Removed the LIFEPAK 35 from service, labeled the unit Out of Service, documented the recurring touchscreen failure, and routed the device for bench repair evaluation.

helpfulDetails: Exact error code or message recorded
Unusual heat, sound, or smell observed

title: Stryker LIFEPAK 35 Defibrillator - Battery Not Charging / Not Recognized
description: Troubleshooting a LIFEPAK 35 battery that does not charge, is not detected, or shows inconsistent battery status despite installation.

steps.title: 1. Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot an unresolved battery or charging problem while the LIFEPAK 35 is supporting an active patient. If battery reliability is uncertain, provide clinical staff with another verified defibrillator before removing the affected unit from service. Expected: Patient care is not dependent on a defibrillator with questionable battery recognition or backup-power capability. Why it matters: A battery fault may reduce portable operating time or leave the device without dependable backup power if external power is interrupted.

steps.title: 2. Verify the Exact Complaint
steps.instructions: Confirm whether the reported condition is: Battery not recognized; Battery icon absent or abnormal; Battery installed but not charging; Battery remains at a low state of charge; One battery position works while the other does not; Charging problem occurs only in the defibrillator; Charging problem also occurs in an approved external charger. Record any displayed message, battery indicator behavior, or warning exactly as shown. Expected: The failure pattern is clearly identified before components are exchanged. If the issue was only a misunderstanding of displayed battery status and normal operation is confirmed, document the finding and stop.

steps.title: 3. Verify External Power and Charging Conditions
steps.instructions: When evaluating an in-device charging complaint: Connect the LIFEPAK 35 to a known-good approved AC power source; Verify the outlet with another appropriate device or outlet tester; Confirm the power connection is fully seated; Inspect the external power cord and accessible power components for damage; Observe whether the device indicates external power operation. Expected: The LIFEPAK 35 receives stable external power required for normal charging evaluation. If restoring a known-good power source resolves charging, verify continued normal operation, document, and stop.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the Battery Externally
steps.instructions: Remove the affected battery from service evaluation and inspect it for: Cracks; Swelling; Deformation; Fluid leakage; Burn marks; Unusual odor; Excessive heat; Damaged or contaminated contacts. Do not continue testing a battery with evidence of physical or thermal damage. Expected: The battery is physically intact and safe for further evaluation. If damage, swelling, leakage, overheating, or burning is found, remove the battery from use and process it according to facility and manufacturer battery-safety procedures. Stop.

steps.title: 5. Remove and Reseat the Battery
steps.instructions: With the device in a safe test condition: Remove the battery. Inspect the accessible battery interface. Reinstall the battery fully. Confirm it mechanically seats and latches correctly. Recheck battery recognition. Expected: A properly installed battery is consistently detected. Why it matters: Partial insertion or incomplete seating can mimic an electronic recognition failure. If reseating restores reliable detection, perform an operational verification, document, and stop.

steps.title: 6. Inspect Accessible Battery and Device Contacts
steps.instructions: Examine the battery contacts and accessible contacts in the battery compartment for: Dirt; Debris; Residue; Corrosion; Bent or visibly damaged contact surfaces; Foreign material preventing full seating. Clean only within approved facility and manufacturer practices. Do not insert tools deeply into the battery compartment or attempt contact repair beyond authorized service scope. Expected: Contact surfaces are clean, unobstructed, and visibly intact. If correcting accessible contamination restores recognition or charging, verify stable operation, document, and stop.

steps.title: 7. Cross-Test With a Known-Good Compatible Battery
steps.instructions: Install a known-good, adequately charged, compatible LIFEPAK 35 battery. Observe whether the device: Recognizes the known-good battery; Displays expected battery status; Begins normal charging behavior when external power is applied; Maintains recognition when the device is gently handled under normal conditions. Expected: A known-good battery is detected consistently. Interpretation: Known-good battery works: Suspect the original battery. Known-good battery also fails: Suspect the device-side battery interface, charging path, power subsystem, or another internal fault. If replacing the defective battery resolves the issue, complete functional verification, document, and stop.

steps.title: 8. Test the Suspect Battery in the Other Battery Position
steps.instructions: Because the LIFEPAK 35 uses a dual-battery configuration, compare behavior between available battery positions when safe and appropriate. Stryker identifies the LIFEPAK 35 as using a dual FLEX lithium-ion battery system. Test systematically: Same battery in position 1; Same battery in position 2; Known-good battery in position 1; Known-good battery in position 2. Expected: The battery is recognized consistently in both functional positions. Interpretation: Failure follows the battery → suspect battery; Multiple batteries fail in one position only → suspect that device-side battery position or interface; Multiple batteries fail in both positions → suspect charging, power, or internal system fault. If the fault is isolated to a battery, replace or remove that battery from service, verify device operation, document, and stop.

steps.title: 9. Compare In-Device Charging With an Approved External Charger
steps.instructions: When an approved LIFEPAK 35 battery charger is available, compare the suspect battery’s behavior outside the defibrillator. Stryker states that typical charging time for one or two fully depleted LIFEPAK 35 batteries is approximately five hours using either the battery charger or the defibrillator. Expected: A serviceable battery demonstrates normal charging behavior in an approved charging environment. Interpretation: Battery charges externally but not in the LIFEPAK 35 → suspect device-side charging or power path; Battery fails in both device and approved charger → suspect battery; Multiple known-good batteries fail only in the LIFEPAK 35 → suspect internal device fault. Do not declare a battery defective solely because it does not immediately show full charge; allow for the normal charging process and evaluate the actual status behavior.

steps.title: 10. Power-Cycle and Recheck Recognition
steps.instructions: After confirming safe conditions and removing the device from clinical reliance: Shut the LIFEPAK 35 down normally. Ensure batteries are properly installed. Restore the intended test power configuration. Restart the unit. Observe battery detection and charging status. Expected: Battery recognition remains stable after restart. If the issue clears but later recurs, do not treat a single successful restart as proof of repair. Continue evaluation or escalate.

steps.title: 11. Review Available Device Status and Fault Information
steps.instructions: Check available device status information, service indications, event information, or fault history within Clinical Engineering authorization. Look for patterns such as: Repeated battery detection failures; Charging-related faults; Power subsystem warnings; Failure isolated to one battery position; Recurrence following movement or power cycling. Expected: Available fault information supports isolation of a battery-specific versus device-specific problem. Do not clear recurring fault information and return the defibrillator to service without determining whether the problem has actually been resolved.

steps.title: 12. Perform a Controlled Operational Verification
steps.instructions: After any apparent correction: Confirm both intended battery positions recognize known-good batteries; Verify stable operation on battery power; Verify external-power operation; Confirm expected charging indication; Observe for intermittent recognition loss; Complete applicable facility operational testing; Perform manufacturer-required inspection or performance procedures when indicated and within authorized service scope. Stryker publishes dedicated LIFEPAK 35 service and performance inspection documentation for authorized technical evaluation. Expected: Battery recognition and charging remain stable throughout controlled testing. If all required checks pass, return the device to service according to facility policy, document, and stop.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported that the Stryker LIFEPAK 35 did not recognize an installed battery and the battery showed no normal charging status.
CCR.Cause: Troubleshooting found that the suspect battery failed recognition in both battery positions while a known-good compatible battery was recognized normally.
CCR.Resolution: Removed the defective battery from service, installed a verified compatible battery, confirmed normal recognition and charging indication, and completed operational testing successfully.

helpfulDetails: Suspect battery tested in approved external charger
Exact warning or battery indication recorded

title: Stryker LIFEPAK 35 Defibrillator - Failed Self-Test / Device Not Ready
description: Troubleshooting failed startup, Auto Test, or readiness checks caused by power, battery, accessory, connection, configuration, or persistent internal faults.

steps.title: 1. Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot a LIFEPAK 35 with a failed self-test or unresolved readiness condition while it is supporting an active patient. Provide clinical staff with another verified defibrillator/monitor before removing the affected unit from service. Expected: Patient care continues with a known-good device. Why it matters: The LIFEPAK 35 provides critical monitoring and therapy functions; unresolved readiness faults must be evaluated away from active patient care.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Exact Failure and Readiness Indication
steps.instructions: Power on the device and document the actual observed condition: Startup failure or incomplete boot; Service wrench LED remaining illuminated; Failed Auto Test; Failed SHIFT Check item; On-screen warning or fault message; Unexpected shutdown or reboot; Abnormal battery or auxiliary-power indication.
